record.tranche_reason: Tests how interventions on layer execution and inference phase affect harmful-response and refusal behavior, using routing changes rather than the fine-tuning, token-position KL, or opening-bypass methods in the claim versions.
record.gate_note: The paper measures response safety under adaptive layer routing and controlled layer-restoration interventions. Those results concern the claim’s broader subject, but do not measure any of its specifically defined versions. The paper also cites prior work on first-token safety concentration; cited results are not recorded here.
record.test_reason: The study measures how token-level layer skipping and restoration change harmful-response and refusal rates in Llama-3-8B-Instruct-based adaptive models. None of this tests a version. There is no harmful or benign fine-tuning, no per-token KL between aligned and base models, and no compliant-opening prefill, suffix or decoding-strategy attack. The 'prefill' here means prompt-processing computation, not a forced response opening. Weight or rank localization of safety is not studied; the paper varies the execution path, not parameters. Qi et al. is cited only in related work. The reader's 'tests'/T2 contradicts its own finding that no version is tested, so it is corrected to cites_only/T6. SafeDepth results are the study's own method.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that token-level adaptive execution degrades backbone safety, with effects depending on inference phase and layer. They propose SafeDepth, a frozen-backbone router trained with safety feedback, which lowers unsafe responses and computation versus FlexiDepth.
record.recipe_differences: The study examines adaptive layer execution, phase-specific layer restoration, and route training; it does not use the cited fine-tuning, per-token KL, compliant-prefill, or suffix methods. SafeDepth trains a router and adapters for execution choices.
record.method_sensitivity: Results vary with whether computation is restored during prefill or decoding and with the specific layer restored. Restoring prefill lowers harmful-response rates more consistently than restoring decoding; equal-sized layer interventions produce different outcomes.

fits_no_version.finding: Token-level adaptive layer skipping raises harmful-response rates over the full-depth backbone: WildJailbreak 8.33% to 41.67% for FlexiDepth and 31.25% for DiffSkip. Restoring skipped computation during prompt processing lowers harm more than restoring it during decoding.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Safety behaviour of aligned models is sensitive to which layers execute and in which inference phase, under adaptive-depth inference.

fits_no_version.finding: Restoring single layers has layer-dependent effects: layers 18 and 20 in prefill reduce harm from 50% to 21.9%, while layer 32 does not. A single later-layer route flip reversed refusal in 7 prompt–layer pairs; 170 pairs were unchanged.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Refusal depends on specific later-layer computation even after harmful intent is linearly decodable at intermediate layers.

fits_no_version.finding: A linear probe on the final input token reaches harmfulness AUROC 0.946 at layer 16. 62 of 200 harmful prompts have a positive danger margin at layer 20 yet still end harmful. This result is not captured in the rows.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Harmfulness recognition and refusal execution are dissociable in internal computation.

record.problems: No uncertainty estimates are reported for the safety outcomes. Some layer-specific findings are described in text alongside figures rather than tabulated. The study uses WildGuard for its reported response scoring; no alternative safety judge is reported for these results.
record.rows_left_out: Omitted the other Table 1 benchmark/model safety rates, the Qwen-based ARM and Plan-and-Budget comparisons in Appendix A.1, and the cross-prompt residual-transfer example in Appendix A.4 to prioritize the directly described phase/layer interventions and the matched Llama reference/adaptive results. Table 3 capability metrics are outside the claim.

untested.parts: No per-token KL between aligned and base models across response positions.
No compliant-opening prefill, adversarial suffix or decoding-strategy attack. Layer skipping and restoration is a different intervention.
No test of safety localized in a small set of weights or ranks. Single-layer route flips concern the execution path, not parameter localization.
No test of data or training-objective causes of shallowness.
No training that spreads safety beyond the first tokens. SafeDepth trains a router, not deeper alignment.

record.verdict_notes: Prefill in this paper means executing layers during prompt encoding, not prefilling a compliant response start, so V4 does not apply. All safety scores come from a single judge (WildGuard). No uncertainty estimates are reported.

versions.untested_parts: No fine-tuning on harmful examples or measurement of how many such examples remove refusal.
No fine-tuning on ordinary or carefully selected benign examples to measure harmful compliance.
No per-token KL comparison between aligned and base models.
No compliant-opening prefills, adversarial suffixes, or decoding-method changes intended to bypass refusal; restoring skipped layers is a different intervention.
No test of whether safety is localized in a small set of weights or ranks.
No test of whether data or training objectives produce first-token shallowness.
No test of training that spreads safety beyond the first response tokens or of its durability.

relation.reason: Section 2 cites Qi et al. for first-token concentration as related work; the study neither tests that finding nor uses it as an experimental tool.

tranche.reason: The study tests safety under adaptive layer execution and restoration, rather than any listed claim version. Layer execution sensitivity does not establish safety localization to a small set of weights or ranks, and router safety training does not test spreading alignment beyond opening response tokens.

source_check.notes: The recorded authors' conclusion matches the text. Prefill restoration concerns prompt processing; Table 6 labels JailbreakBench without identifying the Attacks subset used in Table 1.
